notes.meaning: Even though David knew God had promised him the throne, he did not rush ahead to seize power. Instead, he asked the Lord for guidance on where to go, using the high priest to seek God's will. God directed him to Hebron, an important city in his home territory of Judah with sacred memories of the patriarchs.

David obeyed God right away and brought his wives and loyal followers with him to settle in and around Hebron. These men had stood by David through all his difficult years on the run from Saul. Now they and their families shared in his new home and safety.

The leaders of Judah came to Hebron and publicly recognized David as their king by pouring oil on him, which is called anointing. David had already been chosen by God years earlier, but this was the first time a whole tribe welcomed his rule. While there, David also learned that the brave men of Jabesh-gilead had rescued and buried Saul's body.

differ.view: Some Pentecostal teachers see David's repeated anointings as a picture of believers needing fresh anointings and continual experiences of the Holy Spirit throughout life.

notes.meaning: David sent messengers to bless the people of Jabesh-gilead for their courage and loyalty to Saul. Even though Saul had hunted David for years, David honored the fallen king and those who cared for his remains. True godliness shows genuine honor to others, even former enemies.

David prayed that the Lord would reward the people of Jabesh-gilead with loyal love and faithfulness for what they had done. He also promised that he would treat them with the same kindness and protection. David showed that his gratitude went beyond warm words to real actions.

David urged the town to be strong and brave now that Saul was dead and Judah had crowned him. Saul's army had scattered, and the Philistines were still dangerous, so these men needed courage to stand firm. David was also gently inviting them to trust him as their new protector and leader.

Saul's army commander, Abner, refused to accept David and set up Saul's weak son Ish-bosheth as a rival king instead. Abner took him across the Jordan River to Mahanaim, far away from Philistine attacks and David's home area. From there, Abner pushed Ish-bosheth's claim over the northern and eastern tribes, acting out of personal ambition and family pride.

Ish-bosheth was forty years old and officially reigned for only two years over Israel, while David reigned in Hebron over Judah for seven and a half years. It likely took Abner about five years to clear out the Philistines before he could finally crown Ish-bosheth over the northern tribes. During all these years, David patiently waited on God's timing rather than forcing his way to the whole throne.

Abner marched his army west to Gibeon to expand Ish-bosheth's control, and David's general Joab marched out to meet him. The two forces faced each other across a large stone water pool in the land of Benjamin. Both sides paused there, giving each army time to watch the other and consider what to do next.

Abner suggested that each side pick twelve young warriors to fight in front of the armies as a contest. Calling bloody combat 'playing' showed a reckless disregard for human life. Joab accepted the challenge so his men would not look weak or afraid.

Twelve men from each side stepped forward, grabbed each other by the hair, and stabbed each other at the exact same moment. Every one of the twenty-four champions died on the spot. Because neither side gave way, the battlefield was named Helkath-hazzurim, which means the field of sharp edges or rocky men.

Because the duel ended in a tie, a full and fierce battle broke out between the two armies. God gave the victory to David's men, and Abner's army was thoroughly routed. Starting fights carelessly often brings sudden and terrible defeat.

Joab's brother Asahel was known for running as fast as a wild gazelle. When Abner ran from the battlefield, Asahel chased directly after him, refusing to look at any other enemy. Asahel hoped to end the war at once by capturing or killing the enemy commander.

Abner glanced back and realized who was chasing him. He warned Asahel twice to turn away and fight an ordinary soldier instead of forcing Abner to kill him. Abner wanted to avoid a deadly blood feud with Asahel's brother Joab, David's top general.

Asahel was too proud to turn back, so Abner drove the pointed butt end of his spear straight through him. Asahel died instantly where he fell, showing that physical gifts like speed cannot save someone who acts foolishly. The sight was so shocking that every pursuing soldier stopped in his tracks to mourn.

Joab and his brother Abishai were filled with grief and fury, so they kept chasing Abner until the sun went down. Meanwhile, soldiers from the tribe of Benjamin rallied around Abner on top of a hill. From that high ground, Abner's remaining forces prepared to make a desperate final stand.

Realizing his men were cornered, Abner shouted across the field to Joab, asking if the killing had to go on forever. He reminded Joab that civil war between fellow Israelites would only leave bitterness and sorrow for everyone in the end. People who eagerly start fights often become lovers of peace as soon as they start losing.

Joab swore an oath that Abner himself had caused all the bloodshed by proposing the morning contest. If Abner had not challenged them, Joab's men would have gone home peacefully without striking a single blow. Those who start trouble often blame others when the consequences turn against them.

Joab blew the ram's horn to sound a retreat, and all his troops stopped fighting immediately. Joab showed mercy and discipline by refusing to wipe out fellow Israelites whose leader had made a terrible mistake. David's men were careful not to shed more blood than was necessary.

Abner and his surviving soldiers marched all night through the Jordan Valley to get away safely. They crossed the river and traveled through the hills until they reached Ish-bosheth's stronghold at Mahanaim. Their long retreat marked a humiliating end to the campaign they had started.

When Joab counted his men, only twenty were dead, including his brother Asahel. In contrast, Abner had lost three hundred and sixty soldiers. David's seasoned troops easily overpowered the broken remnants of Saul's old army, showing God's hand on David's cause.

Joab's men lovingly carried Asahel's body back to Bethlehem and buried him in the family tomb. Joab and his soldiers then marched through the rest of the night, arriving back in Hebron just as the sun rose. Though David's men had won the battle, the loss of Asahel cast a dark shadow over their victory.
